messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 69

He first remembers the day of the bombing as a day that should have felt ordinary. He is 37, a South Asian man, married, and working as a psychologist in a busy urban clinic, and at the time he is moving between sessions with the steady rhythm he has built his life around. He is used to listening closely to other people’s fear, grief, and shame; he is the one who helps others make sense of pain. Because of that, the attack feels especially violating. He has built his career around the belief that words and witness can help contain suffering, and in a single moment that belief is shattered by fire, shouting, and the disorienting force of something he cannot reason his way out of.

When the blast occurs, he is far enough away to survive, but close enough to hear the impact, see people running, and feel the strange silence that comes after the worst noise he has ever heard. In the first seconds he is not thinking clinically or clearly. He is thinking in fragments: where is the danger, who is hurt, is his wife safe, can he get out. He remembers his body moving before his mind does, his heart pounding so hard he feels it in his throat, his hands shaking as he tries to help someone he does not know. The smoke has a chemical taste. Sirens arrive too late to make him feel safe.

In the days afterward, he is stunned by how much the world changes without changing at all. The clinic is still there. His notes are still on his desk. Patients still arrive with the same ordinary worries. Yet he begins to feel as though he is moving through someone else’s life. He cannot concentrate during sessions. He catches himself staring at the door, listening for sounds that do not belong. More than once he realizes he has missed part of what a patient has said and has to ask them to repeat it, embarrassed by how far away he feels. He tells himself he is fine, that he understands trauma, that he knows the literature and has spent years helping others through it. But knowledge does not stop his body from reacting as if danger is still nearby.

At home, his wife notices that he startles at the smallest sudden sounds: a car backfiring, a dropped pan, a motorbike passing too close to the apartment. He begins sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants and public places, scanning entrances before he can relax enough to eat. Crowds, once merely tiring, now feel hostile and unpredictable. He makes excuses to avoid markets, public transit, and crowded streets. On his commute he is always aware of exits. He does not say that he is afraid, but his choices make the fear visible. He is ashamed of that fear, especially because of his profession. He has spent years encouraging patients to stay with difficult memories, yet he now works hard to keep his own memory at bay.

At night the image returns. Sometimes it is the blast itself; sometimes it is the look on a stranger’s face, or the smell of smoke, or the sight of shoes scattered across the pavement. He wakes abruptly, drenched in sweat, unable to tell for a moment whether he is home or back there. Sleep becomes something he approaches with reluctance. He lies awake replaying what he saw and what he failed to do, wondering whether he should have moved faster, helped more, remembered better. Even though he knows logically that he was one person in a chaotic scene, his mind keeps returning to guilt. He feels responsible for not being enough.

He also notices that he is no longer fully present with the people he loves. His wife says he seems distant, and he hears the hurt in her voice, which makes him withdraw more. He is shorter with colleagues, less patient with small delays, and finds himself irritated by noise, interruptions, and the casual confidence of people who have not seen what he has seen. Sometimes he feels a surge of anger that surprises him. At other times he feels numb, as if his emotions have been wrapped in thick cloth. He continues to function, continues seeing patients, continues offering calm, but the effort leaves him drained. By the end of the day he feels as though he has been holding himself together with force.

What troubles him most is that he can no longer trust the basic feeling of safety that once organized his life. The world now seems capable of exploding without warning. He checks news updates compulsively, drawn to stories about violence and then sickened by them. He avoids anything that reminds him too directly of the attack, but reminders find him anyway in crowded streets, in sirens, in sudden loud voices, in the smell of smoke from a cooking fire. Each reminder pulls him back into the same tight corridor of fear, as if the event has not finished happening. He is trying, still, to keep his life intact, but his days are increasingly shaped by vigilance, exhaustion, and the sense that part of him remains stranded at the scene of the bombing.
